Jerusalem Again Besieged.<div eID="gen5142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3606"/><hi type="bold">1. Nebuchadnezzar ... came ... against Jerusalem--</hi>Incensed by the revolt of Zedekiah, the Assyrian despot determined to put an end to the perfidious and inconstant monarchy of Judea. This chapter narrates his third and last invasion, which he conducted in person at the head of an immense army, levied out of all the tributary nations under his sway. Having overrun the northern parts of the country and taken almost all the fenced cities (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jr 34:7</reference>), he marched direct to Jerusalem to invest it. The date of the beginning as well as the end of the siege is here carefully marked (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jr 39:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.6">52:4-6</reference>); from which it appears, that, with a brief interruption caused by Nebuchadnezzar's marching to oppose the Egyptians who were coming to its relief but who retreated without fighting, the siege lasted a year and a half. So long a resistance was owing, not to the superior skill and valor of the Jewish soldiers, but to the strength of the city fortifications, on which the king too confidently relied (compare Jr 21:1-14; 37:1-38:28).<div eID="gen5143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pitched against it, and ... built forts--</hi>rather, perhaps, drew lines of circumvallation, with a ditch to prevent any going out of the city. On this rampart were erected his military engines for throwing missiles into the city. <div eID="gen5144" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3607"/><div sID="gen5145" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3607"/><hi type="bold">3. on the ninth day of the fourth month the famine prevailed--</hi>In consequence of the close and protracted blockade, the inhabitants were reduced to dreadful extremities; and under the maddening influence of hunger, the most inhuman atrocities were perpetrated (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">La 2:20</reference>, 22; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Eze 5:10</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3609"/><div sID="gen5150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3609"/><hi type="bold">6-7. they took the king, and brought him ... to Riblah--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar, having gone from the siege to oppose the auxiliary forces of Pharaoh-hophra, left his generals to carry on the blockade, he himself not returning to the scene of action, but taking up his station at Riblah in the land of Hamath (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33">2Ki 23:33</reference>).<div eID="gen5150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they gave judgment upon him--</hi>They, that is, the council (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jr 39:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">Da 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">8, 12</reference>), regarding him as a seditious and rebellious vassal, condemned him for violating his oath and neglecting the announcement of the divine will as made known to him by Jeremiah (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jr 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2">34:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">38:17</reference>). His sons and the nobles who had joined in his flight were slain before his eyes (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jr 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">52:10</reference>). In conformity with Eastern ideas, which consider a blind man incapable of ruling, his eyes were put out, and being put in chains, he was carried to perpetual imprisonment in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jr 52:11</reference>), which, though he came to it, as Ezekiel had foretold, he did not see (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jr 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.16">17:16</reference>). <div eID="gen5151" type="x-p"/>

In conformity with Eastern ideas, which consider a blind man incapable of ruling, his eyes were put out, and being put in chains, he was carried to perpetual imprisonment in Babylon ( Jr 52:11 ), which, though he came to it, as Ezekiel had foretold, he did not see ( Jr 32:5 ; Eze 12:13 ; 17:16 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3610"/><div sID="gen5152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3610"/><hi type="bold">8-18. on the seventh day of the month ... came Nebuzar-adan--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jr 52:12</reference>). In attempting to reconcile these two passages, it must be supposed either that, though he had set out on the seventh, he did not arrive in Jerusalem till the tenth, or that he did not put his orders in execution till that day. His office as captain of the guard (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Ge 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.39.1">39:1</reference>) called him to execute the awards of justice on criminals; and hence, although not engaged in the siege of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.13">Jr 39:13</reference>), Nebuzar-adan was despatched to rase the city, to plunder the temple, to lay both in ruins, demolish the fortifications, and transport the inhabitants to Babylon. The most eminent of these were taken to the king at Riblah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27">2Ki 25:27</reference>) and executed, as instigators and abettors of the rebellion, or otherwise obnoxious to the Assyrian government. In their number were Seraiah, the high priest, grandfather of Ezra (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.1">Ezr 7:1</reference>), his sagan or deputy, a priest of the second order (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jr 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">29:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">37:3</reference>). <div eID="gen5152" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3613"/><div sID="gen5155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3613"/><hi type="bold">22-26. Nebuchadnezzar ... made Gedaliah ... ruler--</hi>The people permitted to remain were, besides the king's daughters, a few court attendants and others (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.7">Jr 40:7</reference>) too insignificant to be removed, only the peasantry who could till the land and dress the vineyards. Gedaliah was Jeremiah's friend (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jr 26:24</reference>), and having, by the prophet's counsel, probably fled from the city as abandoned of God, he surrendered himself to the conqueror (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">17</reference>), and being promoted to the government of Judea, fixed his provincial court at Mizpeh. He was well qualified to surmount the difficulties of ruling at such a crisis. Many of the fugitive Jews, as well as the soldiers of Zedekiah who had accompanied the king in his flight to the plains of Jericho, left their retreats (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.11">Jr 40:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.12">12</reference>) and flocked around the governor; who having counselled them to submit, promised them on complying with this condition, security on oath that they would retain their possessions and enjoy the produce of their land (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.9">Jr 40:9</reference>). <div eID="gen5155" type="x-p"/>

This kindly feeling is said to have originated in a familiar acquaintance formed in prison, in which Evil-merodach had lain till his father's death, on account of some malversation while acting as regent during Nebuchadnezzar's seven years' illness (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.32">Da 4:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">33</reference>). But doubtless the improvement in Zedekiah's condition is to be traced to the overruling providence and grace of Him who still cherished purposes of love to the house of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2Sa 7:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen5159" type="x-p"/>
